question.text: A market maker in interest rate options wants to maintain a market-neutral position. Which Greek should the market maker primarily monitor and manage?

answer.text: Delta, by continuously rebalancing the hedge to maintain a delta-neutral position
Vega, by ensuring all positions have zero sensitivity to volatility
Theta, by ensuring the portfolio has zero time decay
Rho, by ensuring the portfolio is insensitive to rate changes

explanation.text: The Logic: Delta measures the change in option premium for a unit change in the underlying price and is the largest first-order risk in an option book. A market maker who wants to be market-neutral therefore monitors and continuously rebalances delta — adding or trimming offsetting positions in the underlying as prices move — so the book remains insensitive to small directional moves and profits primarily come from the bid-ask spread rather than directional bets. The Trap: Vega manages volatility risk, Theta manages time-decay, and Rho manages interest-rate sensitivity. All are real exposures, but none represents the immediate directional risk that arises tick-by-tick as the underlying moves. Trying to first zero those out instead of delta leaves the book directionally exposed. Note: The cited workbook (NISM Series IV, pages 137-140 and 154) states Delta is the most important Greek and measures option sensitivity to small underlying price changes, but does not explicitly cover market-maker delta-neutral rebalancing — and page 154 notes that market makers are currently not applicable to exchange-traded IRO. The framing above is standard options-market-making knowledge.
